notes.html: Adult worms (females 20 to 35 cm; males 15 to 30 cm) (1) live in the lumen of the small intestine. A female may produce approximately 200,000 eggs per day, which are passed with the faeces (2). Unfertilized eggs may be ingested but are not infective. Fertile eggs embryonate and become infective after 18 days to several weeks (3), depending on the environmental conditions (optimum: moist, warm, shaded soil). After infective eggs are swallowed (4), the larvae hatch (5), invade the intestinal mucosa, and are carried via the portal, then systemic circulation to the lungs (6). The larvae mature further in the lungs (10 to 14 days), penetrate the alveolar walls, ascend the bronchial tree to the throat, and are swallowed (7). Upon reaching the small intestine, they develop into adult worms (1). Between two and three months are required from ingestion of the infective eggs to oviposition by the adult female. Adult worms can live one to two years.

A 48-year-old woman reports fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, and hair loss for 6 months. On exam: pale face, bradycardia (55 bpm), puffy features, delayed reflexes and a firm, small goiter. Lab results: TSH 12 mIU/L (elevated), FT4 0.6 ng/dL (low), anti-TPO antibodies positive

A 38-year-old woman consults for pain in the anterior neck radiating to the jaw for 10 days. She reports fatigue, low-grade fever, and palpitations • On examination: the thyroid is painful, firm, and moderately enlarged. No ophthalmopathy or lymphadenopathy • TSH is low, FT4 is high, ESR is elevated, and anti-TPO antibodies are negative. Thyroid scintigraphy shows low uptake

A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive neck swelling over several months • She complains of difficulty swallowing and a mild change in voice • On examination, the thyroid is very hard, fixed, and painless, with no cervical lymphadenopathy • Thyroid function tests show slightly increased TSH and normal FT4 • Ultrasound reveals a hypoechoic, irregular mass invading adjacent tissues Fine-needle aspiration is non-diagnostic (fibrous tissue only)

A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with unintentional weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance, and tremor over the past three months. On examination, she has diffuse goiter, exophthalmos, lid lag, and a fine tremor of the hands. Her pulse is 110 bpm, and blood pressure is 135/80 mmHg. Laboratory tests reveal: •TSH: <0.01 mIU/L (low) •Free T4: 3.2 ng/dL (elevated) •TSH receptor antibodies: positive
